diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At least in all cases of oligozoospermia or azoospermia.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess sperm production.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During infertility evaluation.

conditions.name: hyperprolactinaemia
conditions.description: An endocrine condition for which the guideline discusses treatment to improve sperm quality when the diagnosis is proven.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish the condition before considering dopamine agonist therapy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When this endocrine cause is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline specifies proven hyperprolactinaemia but does not provide a test method or diagnostic threshold.

special_populations.considerations: A persistently smaller testis is defined by a size difference of >2 ml or 20%, confirmed at two subsequent visits 6 mo apart.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer varicocele surgery when this criterion is met.

special_populations.considerations: Hormonal treatment has poor success rates and is not recommended after puberty.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not use hormonal treatment for cryptorchidism.

special_populations.considerations: Management depends on hormonal function and sperm production. A normally functioning contralateral testis supports a different approach from biochemical hypogonadism or impaired spermatogenesis.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer orchidectomy for a unilateral undescended testis when hormonal function and spermatogenesis are normal. If a unilateral or bilateral undescended testis is accompanied by biochemical hypogonadism or spermatogenic failure, offer orchidopexy when technically feasible. When correcting an undescended testis in adulthood, perform a simultaneous testicular biopsy to assess for intratubular germ cell neoplasia in situ.

special_populations.population: Men with a history of cryptorchidism
special_populations.considerations: Unilateral cryptorchidism may also affect the contralateral testis. Paternity rates after unilateral cryptorchidism are nearly equivalent to those in men without cryptorchidism, whereas the rate after bilateral cryptorchidism is 35–53%. The risk of a germ cell tumour is 3.6–7.4 times higher than in the general population, and 2–6% of men with a history of cryptorchidism develop a testicular tumour.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Counsel patients about fertility and tumour risk and encourage regular testicular self-examination.

special_populations.population: Men with testicular cancer who may receive gonadotoxic treatment
special_populations.considerations: Semen quality may already be impaired before treatment. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy are teratogenic; sperm aneuploidy may increase for up to 2 yr after gonadotoxic therapy.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer sperm cryopreservation before gonadotoxic agents or ablative surgery that could impair sperm production or ejaculation. Offer onco-TESE during radical orchidectomy to men with azoospermia or severe semen abnormalities. Use contraception during chemotherapy or radiotherapy and for at least 6 mo after treatment.
conditions: Germ cell malignancy and male infertility

special_populations.considerations: These men have increased risks of hypogonadism, sexual dysfunction, and cardiovascular disease. Hypogonadism risk is greatest at 6–12 mo after treatment, and Leydig cell function may subsequently improve.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Provide multidisciplinary care through a dedicated late-effects clinic and survivorship programme, and assess serum testosterone during management. It is reasonable to defer testosterone therapy until signs or symptoms of testosterone deficiency persist.
conditions: Germ cell malignancy and male infertility

special_populations.considerations: The significance of TM depends on accompanying risk factors. Infertility, bilateral TM, atrophic testes (<12 ml), a history of undescended testes, and TGCT identify groups for whom biopsy may be offered.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Advise self-examination even when no additional risk factors are present. Do not perform testicular biopsy, follow-up scrotal US, biochemical tumour-marker measurement, or abdominal or pelvic computed tomography for isolated TM without associated risk factors. Offer testicular biopsy to infertile men with TM in the specified higher-risk groups.
conditions: Germ cell malignancy and male infertility

special_populations.population: Men with complete AZFa and AZFb microdeletions
special_populations.considerations: Complete deletions involving these regions predict an almost zero likelihood of surgical sperm retrieval.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not perform surgery for sperm retrieval.

special_populations.population: Men with hypogonadism according to parenthood plans
special_populations.considerations: The guidance distinguishes men with congenital or acquired hypogonadotropic hypogonadism who wish to conceive from symptomatic men with primary or secondary hypogonadism who are not considering parenthood.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For men with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism seeking conception, induce spermatogenesis with hCG, human menopausal gonadotropins, recombinant FSH, or highly purified FSH. Provide testosterone therapy to symptomatic men with primary or secondary hypogonadism who are not considering parenthood; do not use testosterone therapy to treat male infertility.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: This summary of the updated 2025 European Association of Urology (EAU) Guidelines on Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH) addresses the assessment, treatment and follow-up of male infertility. The panel identified and appraised new evidence through a structured literature assessment that searched Medline, EMBASE and the Cochrane Libraries. Recommendations prioritise clinically important decisions; their strength reflects benefits and harms, evidence quality and certainty, and patient preferences. The guidelines emphasise comprehensive urological assessment of men seeking fertility care, concurrent assessment of the female partner to inform shared decisions about timing and treatment, and counselling infertile men or men with abnormal semen parameters about associated health risks. The 2025 changes include new sections on exome sequencing and probiotic treatment, alongside substantial revisions to the diagnostic evidence and recommendations. The overview is intended to support clinical use of guidance on diagnosis, classification, treatment and follow-up.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: The article summarises the updated EAU SRH guidance on male infertility for multidisciplinary clinical care, particularly diagnosis, treatment and follow-up. Guidelines convey the best evidence available to experts but cannot guarantee the best outcome or replace individual clinical judgment. Decisions must also reflect each patient's circumstances and values. The guidance is neither mandatory nor a legal standard of care.

document_sections.heading: 2. Methods
document_sections.content: For the 2025 SRH guidelines, the panel identified, assembled and evaluated relevant new literature after a broad review of the guideline's subject areas. A detailed search strategy is available online. Recommendations were formulated around important shared-care decisions. Their strength depends on the relative desirable and undesirable effects of management options, evidence quality and certainty, and the nature and variation of patient preferences. Strong recommendations generally reflect higher-quality evidence and/or a favourable benefit–harm and preference balance. Weak recommendations generally reflect lower-quality evidence and/or uncertainty about benefits, harms or preferences.

document_sections.heading: 3.1. Epidemiology and aetiology
document_sections.content: Infertility means failure to achieve spontaneous pregnancy within 12 mo in a sexually active couple not using contraception. Approximately 15% of couples do not conceive during 12 consecutive months and seek infertility care. Difficulties conceiving affect one in eight couples seeking a first child and one in six seeking a subsequent child. A male-associated factor is identified in 50% of couples who are involuntarily childless, commonly alongside abnormal semen findings. In 30–40% of cases, no male-associated factor explains the impaired sperm parameters; this was historically called idiopathic male infertility. Table 1 presents causes, associated factors and their distribution; Table 2 sets out epidemiology and aetiology recommendations. The table grades as Strong evaluation after 12 consecutive months of regular unprotected intercourse, simultaneous investigation of both partners, and investigation of every man in a couple seeking fertility care.

document_sections.heading: 3.2. Diagnostic workup
document_sections.content: Focused assessment includes medical and reproductive history, physical examination, semen analysis using WHO reference values, and hormonal assessment. Clinical findings and semen parameters may warrant genetic tests or imaging. Semen analysis is central to assessing sperm quality, but it cannot by itself separate fertile from infertile men. One analysis suffices when results meet WHO criteria; abnormalities on at least two analyses warrant further andrological assessment. Table 3 gives semen reference limits and other thresholds. Table 4 summarises diagnostic recommendations. Its Strong recommendations include parallel assessment of the female partner, including ovarian reserve; examination of men seeking fertility care; full medical, reproductive and family history with lifestyle assessment, examination and semen analysis; use of the latest WHO semen manual; and at least two consecutive analyses after an abnormal baseline result. Counselling about associated health risks and measurement of testicular volume with a Prader orchidometer or US carry a Weak rating.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.1. Measurement of oxidative stress
document_sections.content: Oxidative stress affects sperm quality, function and DNA integrity. The resulting DNA damage and reduced integrity are associated with failed fertilisation, impaired embryo development, miscarriage and implantation failure. Poor lifestyle, including smoking, and environmental exposures commonly accompany oxidative stress. Antioxidants and lifestyle changes may reduce fragmentation risk and improve sperm quality, but high-quality RCT evidence is lacking. ROS can be measured by assays such as chemiluminescence, yet testing is not standardised and routine measurement needs validation in well-designed RCTs. The guidelines do not recommend routine ROS testing; Table 4 rates this recommendation Weak.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.2. Measurement of the sperm DNA fragmentation index
document_sections.content: No study has directly and unequivocally established how SDF testing affects management of infertile couples. SDF occurs more often in infertile men, negatively affects natural pregnancy rates, and is associated with worse ART outcomes, including impaired embryo development, miscarriage, recurrent pregnancy loss and birth defects. Several assays exist, but available assessments of sperm DNA integrity may not predict ART outcomes reliably; routine use remains disputed. Evidence nevertheless supports SDF assessment after recurrent pregnancy loss following natural conception, after ART failure, and in unexplained male infertility. Testicular sperm has less SDF than ejaculated sperm, and its use for ICSI in men with high SDF has been associated with potentially better outcomes. A meta-analysis suggested that TESE for ICSI may improve ART outcomes, but substantial heterogeneity led its authors to call for RCT validation. Clinicians may offer testicular sperm for ART individually to fully informed patients with high SDF, explaining the low-quality evidence and discussing the decision with reproductive specialists. In this setting, testicular sperm should be used only after common causes of raised SDF have been excluded and other SDF-reducing treatments have failed. Table 4 rates SDF testing in the specified circumstances Strong and consideration of testicular sperm for ICSI as an experimental option Weak.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.3. Hormonal determinations
document_sections.content: Hypogonadism frequently accompanies male infertility. Biochemical screening is recommended because of longer-term cardiometabolic implications, including metabolic syndrome and increased cardiovascular risk. Basic assessment measures serum total testosterone, FSH and LH; Table 4 gives a Strong rating to measuring at least these hormones in every case of oligozoospermia or azoospermia. FSH generally correlates negatively with spermatogonial number. Among azoospermic men undergoing TESE, however, FSH does not reliably predict spermatogenesis: maturation arrest may coexist with normal FSH and testicular volume. Emerging evidence associates lower preoperative serum AMH with greater likelihood of successful sperm retrieval during mTESE.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.4. Genetic testing
document_sections.content:
Genetic testing is important for care and counselling. Genetic abnormalities appear more frequent as spermatogenic impairment increases, with NOA showing the highest prevalence of chromosomal abnormalities. Karyotype abnormalities are the most prevalent genetic contributors. Numerical abnormalities include the additional X chromosomes of Klinefelter syndrome, whose presentation and preservation of germ cells or spermatogenesis vary; TESE retrieves sperm in 20–50% of cases. Structural abnormalities, including deletions, duplications, inversions and Robertsonian translocation, can impair or eliminate spermatogenesis. Compared with the general population, mainly autosomal structural abnormalities occur tenfold more often among patients with sperm counts <5 million/ml (4%). Men with NOA face the greatest risk, especially of sex-chromosome abnormalities. The guidance advocates karyotyping for azoospermia or sperm concentration <5 million/ml.

Y-chromosome AZFa, AZFb and AZFc microdeletions are the second most common genetic cause. AZFc accounts for 65–70%; AZFb, AZFb + AZFc, or AZFa + AZFb + AZFc regions account for 25–30%; AZFa accounts for 5%. Complete AZFa deletion is associated with SCOS and complete AZFb deletion with spermatogenic arrest. Complete AZFa or AZFb deletions predict poor surgical sperm retrieval, so TESE should not be attempted. AZFc deletion can present with oligospermia or azoospermia; TESE retrieves sperm in 53–75% of affected men. Microdeletions are absent with normal sperm parameters and rare above 5 million/ml. The text recommends testing below <5 million/ml and regards it as mandatory for azoospermia or concentration <1 million/ml. Table 4 prints its Strong recommendation using '1 million sperm/ml' for one testing threshold, without a comparison sign, and also says to consider testing below <5 million sperm/ml. That table also gives Strong ratings to counselling men with Yq microdeletion and their partners that sons conceived through ICSI will inherit it, and to avoiding testicular sperm extraction when complete deletions include AZFa and AZFb.

Cystic fibrosis is described as the commonest autosomal recessive disorder in Caucasian populations. Approximately 2000 CFTR mutations have been identified; any CFTR alteration can cause CBAVD. CBAVD occurs in approximately 1% of infertile men and up to 6% of men with OA. Careful examination for CBAVD is needed in azoospermia, particularly with semen volume <1.0 ml and acidic pH <7.0. Men with unilateral or bilateral absence of the vas deferens without renal agenesis, and their partners, should be tested for CFTR mutations. Table 4 rates testing for CFTR mutations and genetic counselling for couples with identified genetic abnormalities or potentially inheritable disease Strong. It likewise rates offering standard karyotype analysis and genetic counselling in azoospermia or oligozoospermia with spermatozoa <5 million/ml Strong, and long-term endocrine follow-up with appropriate medical treatment for Klinefelter syndrome Strong.

The diagnostic yield of whole-exome sequencing in NOA is increasing, identifying monogenic causes, potentially relevant variants and candidate genes. Case-control series in motility and morphology disorders have identified variants potentially suitable for phenotype-specific panels, underscoring the diagnostic importance of genotyping in severe male-factor infertility. Exome sequencing may improve diagnosis and possibly management in idiopathic infertility and NOA, although its clinical application remains unclear.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.5. Imaging in infertile men
document_sections.content:
The Prader orchidometer provides a practical, less costly approximation of ultrasound-derived testicular volume. Scrotal US remains useful for volume assessment in selected cases, including large hydrocele, inguinal testis, epididymal enlargement or fibrosis, thickened scrotal skin, and a small testis with a proportionally large epididymis. It can assess structural signs of testicular dysgenesis, identify tumours, and detect indirect evidence of obstruction such as rete testis dilatation, cystic epididymal enlargement or an absent vas deferens. Compared with fertile men, infertile men have greater testicular cancer risk (pooled odds ratio [OR] 1.91, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.52–2.42). Compared with fertile controls, oligozoospermic men have a higher cancer risk (hazard ratio 11.9). Testicular cancer prevalence was approximately 18-fold higher among men with TM. The cost–benefit balance of routine US screening in infertility is unclear, and incidental masses can lead to overdiagnosis, surveillance or intervention.

No definitive US size threshold distinguishes benign from malignant lesions, although data suggest lesions < 5 mm are more often benign. In postpubertal men, malignancy odds were significantly lower for heterogeneous rather than homogeneous masses, hyperechogenic rather than hypoechogenic masses, normal rather than elevated enhancement, and peripheral rather than central vascularity. Small abnormal-echo areas may instead represent cysts, focal Leydig-cell hyperplasia, fibrosis or residual focal inhomogeneity. Careful periodic US assessment is needed, particularly with additional malignancy risk factors. Histology remains the clinical standard for distinguishing benign and malignant lesions, but most incidentally detected lesions during infertility assessment are benign, making biopsy potentially excessive. Multidisciplinary assessment should consider risk factors, interval growth and US features such as size >5 mm, echogenicity and vascularity.

Colour Doppler US can corroborate a clinically detected varicocele and measure reflux and vein diameter. Radiologically significant varicoceles have venous diameter >3 mm while upright and during Valsalva, with reflux lasting more than 2 s. Scrotal US also evaluates the vas deferens, seminal vesicles and epididymis. Transrectal US may identify ejaculatory duct cysts, obstruction, dilatation and seminal-vesicle atrophy or hypoplasia in azoospermia. Table 4 gives a Weak rating to scrotal US in infertile men and to multidisciplinary discussion of biopsy, orchidectomy or surveillance for indeterminate lesions, especially with further risk factors; transrectal US for suspected partial or complete distal obstruction is rated Strong.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.1. Cryptorchidism
document_sections.content:
Cryptorchidism affects approximately 1% of infants. It has been proposed as part of TDS, a gonadal developmental disorder potentially influenced by environmental or genetic exposures early in pregnancy, including endocrine-disrupting chemicals. TDS also encompasses hypospadias, reduced fertility, malignancy risk and Leydig/Sertoli-cell dysfunction. Germ-cell loss in undescended testes is evident after the first year of life, varies with testicular position and progresses during the second year. Treatment between 6 mo and 18 mo is recommended to preserve spermatogonial stem cells, future spermatogenesis and hormone production, and to reduce tumour risk. Surgery is most effective; meta-analyses found poor success with GnRH and hCG treatment. The apparently normal contralateral testis in unilateral cryptorchidism can itself have lower volume, softer consistency and reduced markers of future fertility, warranting counselling of patients and parents.

Paternity after unilateral cryptorchidism is nearly comparable to that of men without cryptorchidism; after bilateral cryptorchidism it is 35–53%, which should inform counselling. Men may also face increased hypogonadism and testicular cancer risks and should be encouraged to examine their testes regularly. Germ-cell tumour risk is 3.6–7.4 times that of the general population, and 2–6% of men with prior cryptorchidism develop a testicular tumour. Prepubertal orchidopexy reduces cancer risk, but evidence suggests risk remains above that of men without cryptorchidism even after early surgery.

Adult management depends on hormonal and spermatogenic assessment. Orchidectomy may be offered for a unilateral undescended testis when the opposite testis functions normally, given cancer and GCNIS risk. Where contralateral function is impaired by biochemical hypogonadism and/or impaired sperm production, orchidopexy may preserve androgen production and fertility. On panel consensus, multiple biopsies at adult orchidopexy are recommended to exclude GCNIS, which predicts future TGCT. During orchidectomy for TGCT, contralateral biopsy should be offered to patients at high GCNIS risk, including those with cryptorchidism history, volume <12 ml or hypospermatogenesis. Table 5 rates avoidance of hormonal treatment after puberty, biopsy during adult correction, and orchidectomy for unilateral cryptorchidism with normal hormonal and sperm function Strong. Offering technically feasible orchidopexy for adult unilateral or bilateral undescended testes with hypogonadism or spermatogenic failure is rated Weak.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.2. Germ cell malignancy and male infertility
document_sections.content:
TGCT is the most frequent malignancy among Caucasian men aged 15–40 yr and occurs in approximately 1% of subfertile men. Infertile men have increased risks of testicular and other cancers. Semen quality can be impaired before TGCT treatment: azoospermia has been observed in 24% and oligospermia in 50%. With an average 10-yr testicular cancer survival of 98%, fertility-preservation counselling before gonadotoxic treatment is mandatory. Men with cancer must be offered sperm cryopreservation before gonadotoxic agents or surgery that may impair spermatogenesis or ejaculation, including chemotherapy, radiotherapy and retroperitoneal surgery. Ejaculated-semen preservation should be offered as the most cost-effective option; surgically obtained sperm, including onco-TESE, is an option with severe oligozoospermia or azoospermia. Because chemotherapy and radiotherapy are teratogenic, contraception is required during treatment and for at least 6 mo afterward.

TGCT treatment can further reduce semen quality and raise sperm aneuploidy for up to 2 yr after gonadotoxic therapy. Spermatogenesis generally recovers 1–4 yr after chemotherapy. Chemotherapy is also associated with DNA damage and increased SDF. Aneuploidy frequently falls to pretreatment levels 18–24 mo after therapy. Leydig-cell dysfunction may affect even the contralateral testis. Survivors have higher hypogonadism risk and should have serum testosterone assessed during care. Risk peaks at 6–12 mo after treatment, suggesting that Leydig-cell function may subsequently improve; delaying testosterone therapy until deficiency signs or symptoms persist is therefore reasonable.

TM is detected in 0.6–9% of men referred for testicular US and has been observed alongside TGCT, cryptorchidism, infertility, torsion, atrophy, Klinefelter syndrome, hypogonadism, disorders of sex development and varicocele. In healthy asymptomatic men, TM carries a low concurrent or longer-term risk of TGCT or GCNIS of unclassified type. A meta-analysis found that TM in men with previous subfertility, cryptorchidism or TGCT increased concurrent TGCT risk (risk ratio 8.5, 95% CI 4.5–16.1; p < 0.0001). A systematic review and meta-analysis of case-control studies associated TM with 18-fold higher testicular cancer odds among infertile men (pooled OR 18.11, 95% CI 8.09–40.55; p < 0.0001). The TM–TGCT relationship remains controversial. Proposed higher-risk features for GCNIS include infertility, atrophic or undescended testes, previous TGCT and contralateral TM; biopsy has been suggested for men with these features.

Table 5 rates advice to self-examine with TM, even without other risk factors, Weak. It rates avoidance of biopsy, surveillance scrotal US, biochemical tumour markers and abdominal or pelvic computed tomography for isolated TM without associated risk factors Strong. Offering biopsy for infertile men with TM and specified higher-risk features is Weak; inguinal exploration with biopsy or orchidectomy following multidisciplinary and patient discussion when examination or US is suspicious is Strong. Multidisciplinary late-effects care and survivorship for TGCT survivors, sperm cryopreservation before planned orchidectomy or further oncological treatment, and onco-TESE during radical orchidectomy for testicular cancer with azoospermia or severe semen abnormalities are rated Strong.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.3. Varicocele
document_sections.content:
Varicocele occurs in almost 15% of the general male population, 25% of men with abnormal semen analysis and 35– 40% of men presenting with infertility. Higher grade and age accompany worse semen parameters. Its precise relationship to reduced fertility remains unknown. Increased scrotal temperature, hypoxia and reflux of toxic metabolites may contribute to testicular dysfunction and infertility. Although repair has long been debated, recent meta-analyses associate treatment of clinical varicocele with improved semen parameters, pregnancy and live-birth rates. Semen improvement after surgery is generally seen in men with abnormal preoperative sperm quality. Subclinical varicocele treatment did not increase spontaneous pregnancy, and randomised studies consisting mainly of men with normal semen parameters showed no benefit of treatment over observation. Varicocelectomy may reverse sperm DNA damage and improve oxidative-stress measures. Another meta-analysis suggested better ART outcomes in oligozoospermic men (OR 1.69, 95% CI 0.95–3.02). Mean time to semen-parameter improvement after repair is up to two spermatogenic cycles; spontaneous pregnancy occurs between 6 and 12 mo after varicocelectomy.

Varicocelectomy may result in ejaculated sperm among men with azoospermia. Meta-analyses also reported improved surgical sperm retrieval for clinical varicocele with NOA, particularly with histological hypospermatogenesis. Evidence quality is low. Risks and benefits should be fully discussed before treating NOA with clinically significant varicocele, especially when the female partner has limited ovarian reserve. Varicocelectomy can improve sperm DNA integrity. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 1070 infertile men with clinical varicocele associated surgery with reduced postoperative SDF (weighted mean difference [WMD] 7.23%, 95% CI 8.86% to 5.59%). Improvement did not depend on the specified DNA-integrity assay or surgical technique. The reported WMD was greater in studies with preoperative mean SFD 20% than in those with SDF <20%, suggesting greater potential benefit at higher baseline SDF; effect size increased with preoperative SDF (coefficient 0.23, 95%CI 0.07–0.39).

Evidence is accumulating that treatment may lower DNA fragmentation and improve ART outcomes, supporting consideration after ART failure with high SDF once other infertility causes are excluded. However, there is no cost–benefit analysis for this indication, prospective evidence on SDF, pregnancy and live birth is limited, and benefit with normal conventional semen parameters but abnormal SDF is unclear. The panel recommends counselling infertile patients with clinical varicocele or abnormal semen parameters about possible repair benefits. Treatment may be offered for abnormal SDF outside those circumstances only with counselling about the limited evidence for that indication alone. Microsurgery was associated with the fewest complications and recurrences and the highest spontaneous pregnancy rates, but evidence is insufficient to establish superiority over every other technique. Table 5 rates surgery for adolescents with a persistently smaller testis, a difference of >2 ml or 20% confirmed at two visits 6 mo apart, Strong. It rates avoiding treatment for subclinical varicocele or normal semen analysis Strong, and treating clinical varicocele with abnormal semen parameters and otherwise unexplained infertility when the partner has good ovarian reserve Strong. Considering varicocelectomy for elevated SDF with otherwise unexplained infertility or failed assisted reproduction, including recurrent pregnancy loss or failure of embryogenesis or implantation, is Weak.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.4. Male accessory-gland infections and infertility
document_sections.content:
WHO categorises urethritis, prostatitis, orchitis and epididymitis as male accessory-gland infections. Findings on the influence of symptomatic and asymptomatic infections on sperm quality conflict. A systematic review could not establish a strong sexually transmitted infection–infertility association because available data were limited in quality. Peroxidase-positive white blood cells >106/ml of ejaculate indicate inflammation, termed leukocytospermia, but do not necessarily establish infection. Suspected genitourinary infection warrants semen culture or polymerase chain reaction analysis for common urinary pathogens. Urinary-pathogen concentration >103 CFU/ml in ejaculate indicates significant bacteriospermia.

A meta-analysis of case-control studies found that leukocytospermia in men seeking couple-subfertility care was not associated with poorer ART fertility or altered semen quality in men without genital-infection symptoms. There is no current evidence that treating leukocytospermia alone, without infective organisms, improves conception. Another meta-analysis associated Ureaplasma urealyticum and Myocoplasma hominis, but not Ureoplasma parvum or Mycoplasma genitalium, with male infertility. Human papillomavirus may also be associated with male infertility, but confirmatory prospective research is scarce and benefit from antiviral therapy is unclear. A case-control study suggested that treating asymptomatic Chlamydia may improve sperm parameters, without establishing an effect on conception.

Only antibiotic treatment of chronic bacterial prostatitis, type II under the National Institutes of Health classification, has yielded symptom relief, microbial eradication and reduced cellular and humoral inflammatory measures in urogenital secretions. Antibiotics might improve sperm quality, but treatment of CP/CPPS has not been shown to increase natural conception probability. RCTs with suitable cost–benefit analyses and pregnancy and live-birth outcomes are needed to clarify the role of antibiotics and probiotics. Partners of patients whose accessory sex-gland infections are known or suspected to be sexually transmitted should be referred for assessment and treatment. Table 5 rates treatment of accessory-gland infection as Weak, noting possible sperm-quality improvement without necessarily improving conception; partner referral is Strong.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.1.1. Lifestyle changes
document_sections.content: Weight loss, physical exercise and smoking cessation can improve sperm parameters and should be encouraged; they may also improve general health. This matters because growing evidence links male infertility to cardiometabolic disorders and higher cardiovascular and overall mortality compared with fertile controls. All infertile men should be screened for modifiable cardiovascular risk factors. Urological assessment offers an opportunity to address otherwise unrecognised early disease and potentially improve life expectancy. Table 6 rates counselling about the detrimental effects of obesity, low activity, smoking and high alcohol intake on sperm quality and testosterone, and advice to improve lifestyle to enhance conception chances, Strong.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.1.2. Oxidative stress therapy
document_sections.content: Oxidative stress is regarded as an important contributor to idiopathic male infertility. High seminal ROS is associated with worse sperm parameters, higher SDF and adverse ART outcomes. Evidence for empirical antioxidants remains conflicting. A Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of 61 studies involving 6264 infertile men aged 18–65 yr found that antioxidants may increase live births, but evidence quality was low and the apparent increase disappeared when studies at high risk of bias were excluded. A later systematic review and meta-analysis of 45 RCTs involving 4332 infertile patients found significantly higher sperm concentration, progressive motility, total motility, normal morphology and pregnancy rates with antioxidants than in its specified control groups. There is no clear consensus on optimal constituents or regimen; antioxidants therefore remain empirical pending larger RCTs. Table 6 gives a Weak rating to its recommendation against routine antioxidant treatment for idiopathic infertility.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.1.3. Prebiotic and probiotic supplements
document_sections.content: Prebiotic/probiotic supplementation has been studied for male infertility. An RCT of 56 men with idiopathic infertility compared a prebiotic/probiotic compound with placebo and reported significant improvement in the treated group's sperm concentration, motility and normal morphology, together with greater DNA integrity. Further adequately powered RCTs are needed. Table 6 rates its recommendation against routine prebiotic/probiotic treatment of idiopathic infertility Weak.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.1.4. Hormonal treatment
document_sections.content:
Gonadotropin use in secondary hypogonadism is established. A meta-analysis found ejaculated sperm production in 75% of patients with NOA and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism treated with hCG with or without FSH. Hormonal stimulation in primary hypogonadism or eugonadal idiopathic infertility remains disputed. SERMs block hypothalamic oestrogen receptors, increasing GnRH secretion and pituitary gonadotropin release, with potential stimulation of spermatogenesis. A meta-analysis of 11 RCTs found significant increases in pregnancy rates and sperm and hormonal measures; an updated meta-analysis of 16 studies reported similar findings. Study quality was low and few studies had placebo controls, preventing conclusive recommendations for SERMs in idiopathic infertility.

Aromatase inhibitors may reversibly inhibit cytochrome p450 isoenzymes 2A6 and 2C19 within the aromatase complex, reducing oestrogen production and its hypothalamic negative feedback; stronger GnRH pulses may then stimulate pituitary FSH production. Off-label use has been reported to raise endogenous testosterone and improve spermatogenesis. Steroidal testolactone and nonsteroidal anastrozole and letrozole significantly improved hormonal and semen measures with a safe tolerability profile, although prospective RCTs are required to define efficacy more clearly.

Some evidence supports improved sperm parameters with FSH in idiopathic oligozoospermia and normal FSH, generally 1.5–8 mIU/ml. FSH in idiopathic infertility has been assessed in more than 20 clinical trials summarised by four meta-analyses. Collectively, they suggest dose-dependent, significant increases in sperm concentration and total count, as well as significantly higher spontaneous and ART pregnancy rates; there was no significant difference between ICSI and intrauterine insemination. FSH may also improve SDF, AMH and inhibin measures. A few studies investigated stimulation before TESE in azoospermia. Evidence for FSH/hCG is constrained by few studies and small cohorts, so no clinical recommendation can be made on that basis; large RCTs are needed before routine stimulation can be recommended for eugonadal men or men with NOA.

Table 6 rates inducing spermatogenesis with hCG, human menopausal gonadotropins, recombinant FSH or highly purified FSH in men with congenital or acquired hypogonadotropic hypogonadism who wish to conceive Strong. Its recommendations to use FSH for idiopathic oligozoospermia with normal FSH, avoid high-dose FSH in idiopathic infertility, avoid stimulation before TESE for NOA outside trials, avoid routine SERMs or aromatase inhibitors in idiopathic infertility, offer dopamine agonist therapy for proven hyperprolactinaemia, and withdraw anabolic steroids for 6–12 mo before considering SERMs or gonadotrophins are rated Weak. Avoiding testosterone as infertility treatment and providing it to symptomatic men with primary or secondary hypogonadism who are not pursuing parenthood are rated Strong.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.2.1. Obstructive azoospermia
document_sections.content:
OA accounts for 20–40% of azoospermia and means absent ejaculated sperm because sperm transport is blocked rather than because spermatogenesis is abnormal. Obstruction may be intratesticular, epididymal, vasal, at the ejaculatory duct, or functional in the distal seminal ducts. Typical findings are normal FSH, normal-sized testes and low semen volume; additional findings may include a dilated epididymis, epididymal or vasal nodules, and absent vasa in CBAVD. Management depends on obstruction site and cause. Intratesticular obstruction requires TESE. Epididymal or inguinal vasal obstruction may be managed with microsurgical reconstruction, such as vasoepididymostomy, or sperm retrieval by microsurgical or percutaneous epididymal aspiration or TESE. In OA, ICSI pregnancy outcomes are comparable using epididymal or testicular sperm and using fresh or frozen–thawed epididymal sperm. Microsurgical reversal after vasectomy achieves patency of 90–97%.

Postinflammatory or cystic ejaculatory duct obstruction may be treated by TURED. Pregnancy after TURED occurs in 12.5–31%; counselling must address epididymitis, treatment failure, urinary incontinence and urine reflux into ejaculatory ducts or seminal vesicles. When considering reconstruction for any OA, the female partner's ovarian reserve must inform comparison with sperm retrieval and ICSI. Table 7 rates microsurgical vasovasostomy or epididymovasostomy for appropriate vasal or epididymal obstruction when the partner has good ovarian reserve Strong. It also rates retrieval as an adjunct to reconstruction, when repair is unsuitable, when ovarian reserve is limited, or when the couple prefers direct ICSI over reconstruction Strong.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.2.2. Nonobstructive azoospermia
document_sections.content:
NOA is the absence of ejaculated sperm after centrifugation, reflecting severe spermatogenic impairment associated with primary testicular dysfunction or hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal dysfunction. Confirmation requires at least two consecutive centrifuged semen analyses. Men usually have small testes, normal semen volume and raised FSH. Sperm production can be confined to isolated testicular foci. Across differing cohorts and techniques, positive retrieval after TESE has been reported in up to 50% of patients. No investigated preoperative factor has reliably predicted success. Hypospermatogenesis on biopsy predicted positive TESE retrieval better than maturation arrest or SCOS. Reported associations for FSH, LH, inhibin B and AMH are variable and based on limited retrospective series; findings for testicular volume are inconsistent. Complete AZFa and AZFb microdeletions make retrieval almost impossible, so TESE is contraindicated.

FNA mapping has been proposed to identify promising retrieval sites before TESE and ICSI, but mapping itself obtains no sperm. It can necessitate two operations where one might suffice and delay treatment. No RCT has compared mTESE with versus without mapping, and effective cost–benefit analyses are unavailable. The guidelines therefore do not recommend FNA mapping as a primary diagnostic step before TESE pending prospective comparative studies. Table 7 rates confirmation by two semen analyses, comprehensive assessment of cause and comorbidity, genetic counselling before ART for couples with genetic abnormalities, and retrieval surgery for appropriate ICSI candidates Strong. It rates avoidance of retrieval with complete AZFa and AZFb microdeletions, where the chance of retrieval is zero, and avoidance of FNA and TESA in NOA Strong. Avoiding prognostic FNA mapping before definitive TESE and not treating preoperative clinical or biochemical variables as reliable stand-alone predictors are rated Weak.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.2.3. Conventional and microdissection TESE
document_sections.content:
cTESE retrieves sperm through randomly selected testicular biopsies; single-arm studies report retrieval rates of 50%, while observational studies suggest that taking multiple biopsies raises retrieval chances. cTESE has been associated with more complications than other techniques. mTESE uses operative microscopy to select tubules more likely to contain sperm and limit unintended vascular injury, aiming for better retrieval with less removed tissue and fewer complications. One meta-analysis in NOA found successful retrieval 1.5 times more often with mTESE than cTESE; another found comparable surgical retrieval rates. mTESE has shown fewer haematomas and less fibrosis. Long-term follow-up has shown testosterone recovery to baseline after both procedures. Salvage mTESE retrieved sperm in 46.5% of patients after unsuccessful cTESE or testicular sperm aspiration.

Few RCTs directly compare the procedures. Although the latest comprehensive meta-analysis found no difference in retrieval rates for NOA, every individual comparative trial favoured mTESE for retrieval. Available data also suggest fewer complications after mTESE. The panel's consensus identifies mTESE as the preferred surgical retrieval approach in NOA, while acknowledging low-quality evidence and the need for larger RCTs comparing retrieval, risk and cost. Table 7 rates use of microdissection TESE as the treatment of choice Weak.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.3. Hormonal therapy before surgical SR approaches
document_sections.content: Increasing intratesticular testosterone or serum FSH has been proposed to stimulate spermatogenesis and improve surgical retrieval in NOA. Options studied include hCG, FSH and SERMs, but there is no standardised protocol. No RCT has shown that hormonal treatment improves positive retrieval in idiopathic NOA. A meta-analysis suggested a possible benefit from pre-TESE stimulation in eugonadal men but not in hypergonadotropic hypogonadism; included studies had moderate or severe risk of bias, so randomised confirmation is needed. Table 7 gives a Weak rating to avoiding routine medical treatment, including hormonal stimulation, before conventional TESE or mTESE in NOA with hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism.

document_sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
document_sections.content: This article summarises the 2025 EAU SRH guidance concerning male infertility. A male factor is identifiable in approximately 50% of infertile couples, supporting careful assessment of every infertile man. Growing evidence indicates higher oncological and nononcological comorbidity risks in infertile men, warranting screening and counselling. Several empirical treatments exist, but evidence remains insufficient to support their use in clinical practice. The full EAU guidelines provide further detail and references.
